title: Why We Yawn and Hiccup
summary: Why our bodies make us yawn and hiccup, and what scientists think causes these strange, involuntary habits.
poll: Yawning and hiccups are just silly habits with no real purpose.

versions.title: Yawns and Hiccups
versions.text:
Have you yawned? You open your mouth. You take a big breath. Then you shut your mouth.

People yawn when tired. People yawn when bored too.

Yawns can spread! See someone yawn, and you may yawn too. Read about a yawn, and you may yawn too.

Why do we yawn? No one is fully sure. One idea: a yawn cools your brain. Another idea: it wakes you up.

Now think of hiccups. A hiccup makes a 'hic' sound.

Under your lungs is the diaphragm. It is a muscle. It helps you breathe. Sometimes it jumps by itself.

When it jumps, your throat snaps shut fast. That snap makes the 'hic' sound.

Hiccups can start if you eat fast. Fizzy pop can start them too. They stop on their own. Try a slow stretch. Take a deep breath too.

versions.title: The Mystery of Yawns and Hiccups
versions.text:
Have you ever let out a big yawn? You open your mouth wide and take a deep breath, and then you close your mouth again, often with a sigh.

People often yawn when they are tired or sleepy. They also yawn when they feel bored, even in the middle of a busy day.

Yawning can spread from person to person! If you see someone yawn, or even just hear one, you might yawn too. Even reading about a yawn can make you yawn.

Why do people yawn? Scientists still do not fully agree. One idea is that a yawn helps cool down your brain when it gets a little too warm. Another idea is that yawning helps wake up your brain and body when you need more energy.

Now think about hiccups. A hiccup makes a sudden, funny 'hic' sound that you cannot control, no matter how hard you try.

Under your lungs is a large, flat muscle called the diaphragm. It tightens and relaxes to help you breathe in and out all day long. Sometimes this muscle suddenly jumps, or spasms, all on its own.

When the diaphragm spasms suddenly, a part deep in your throat snaps shut very fast. That quick snap is what makes the 'hic' sound you hear.

Hiccups often start if you eat too fast, laugh hard, or drink a fizzy drink. They usually stop on their own after a few minutes. Sipping water slowly can help them go away faster, and taking a slow stretch with a deep breath can help too.

versions.title: Why We Yawn and Hiccup
versions.text:
Have you ever let out a big yawn? You open your mouth wide and take a deep breath, and then you close your mouth again, often with a tired sigh that follows soon after.

People often yawn when they are tired or sleepy, and they also yawn when they feel bored, even in the middle of a busy, ordinary day.

Yawning is an involuntary reflex, and it is surprisingly contagious. If you see someone yawn, or even just hear one, you are quite likely to yawn too, and even reading about a yawn can trigger one in you, which many people find quite strange and hard to explain.

Why do people yawn? Scientists still do not fully agree on a single explanation, although they have proposed a couple of competing hypotheses over the years. One hypothesis suggests that a yawn helps cool down the brain whenever it becomes a little too warm. Another hypothesis suggests that yawning helps raise your level of alertness whenever your body needs more energy to stay focused and awake.

Now consider hiccups. A hiccup produces a sudden, involuntary 'hic' sound that you cannot control, no matter how hard you try to stop it from happening.

Under your lungs is a large, flat muscle called the diaphragm, which tightens and relaxes continuously to help you breathe in and out. It is controlled by a nerve called the phrenic nerve, and sometimes this nerve sends a confused signal that makes the diaphragm spasm suddenly and without any clear warning at all.

When the diaphragm spasms, the glottis, a small opening between your vocal cords, snaps shut very quickly. That quick snap is what produces the distinctive 'hic' sound you hear.

Common triggers for hiccups include eating too quickly, laughing hard, or drinking a fizzy, carbonated drink. They usually stop on their own within a few minutes, and sipping water slowly, along with a slow stretch and a deep breath, can help them go away faster.

Yawning is an involuntary reflex, and it is surprisingly contagious. Seeing someone yawn, or even just hearing one, is often enough to trigger a yawn in return, and even reading about yawning can have precisely the same curious effect on many readers.

Why do people yawn? Scientists still do not fully agree on a single explanation, although two competing hypotheses have been proposed by researchers over the years. One hypothesis suggests that a yawn helps cool down the brain whenever it becomes slightly too warm. Another hypothesis suggests that yawning helps raise the body's level of alertness whenever more energy and focus are needed.

Now consider hiccups. A hiccup produces a sudden, involuntary 'hic' sound that cannot be controlled, no matter how hard a person tries to stop it from happening.

Beneath the lungs lies a large, flat muscle called the diaphragm, which tightens and relaxes continuously to assist breathing throughout each and every day. This muscle is controlled by the phrenic nerve, and occasionally that nerve sends a confused signal that makes the diaphragm spasm suddenly and unexpectedly.

When the diaphragm spasms, the glottis, a small opening between the vocal cords, snaps shut very quickly. That rapid snap is what produces the distinctive 'hic' sound that everyone recognizes.

Common triggers for hiccups include eating too quickly, laughing hard, or drinking a fizzy, carbonated beverage, among several other everyday causes. They usually stop on their own within a few minutes, and sipping water slowly, along with a slow stretch and a deep breath, can help them go away faster than they otherwise would.

versions.title: Why We Yawn and Hiccup
versions.text:
Placing a hand near the mouth during a yawn reveals a wide stretch of the jaw and a deep, drawn-out breath, a combination that makes this common behavior more mysterious than it first appears.

People tend to yawn when they are tired or sleepy, and they also yawn when they feel bored, even in the middle of an ordinary, busy day.

Yawning is an involuntary reflex, and it is remarkably contagious, since seeing someone yawn, or even hearing one, is often enough to trigger a yawn in return, and simply reading a description of yawning can produce the very same effect. Even some animals, including dogs and chimpanzees, sometimes yawn after watching a person yawn, which suggests that this behavior may have deep biological roots.

Why do people yawn? Scientists still do not fully agree on a single explanation, although two main hypotheses have been proposed. One hypothesis suggests that a yawn helps cool the brain whenever its temperature rises slightly above normal, much like a tiny internal fan. Another hypothesis suggests that yawning raises the body's overall level of alertness whenever additional energy and focus are needed, perhaps by stretching the jaw muscles and increasing blood flow to the face.

Now consider hiccups, a very different but equally puzzling reflex. A hiccup produces a sudden, involuntary "hic" sound that cannot be controlled, no matter how determined a person is to stop it.

Beneath the lungs lies a large, flat muscle called the diaphragm, which tightens and relaxes continuously to assist breathing throughout the day, expanding the chest to pull air in and relaxing to let air back out. This essential muscle is controlled by the phrenic nerve, and occasionally that nerve transmits a confused signal that makes the diaphragm spasm without warning.

When the diaphragm suddenly spasms, the glottis, a small opening located between the vocal cords, snaps shut very quickly, cutting off the sudden rush of air. That rapid, forceful snap is precisely what produces the distinctive "hic" sound that everyone recognizes.

Common triggers for hiccups include eating too quickly, laughing hard, or drinking a fizzy, carbonated beverage, all of which can irritate the diaphragm or the nerve that controls it. They usually stop on their own within a few minutes, and sipping water slowly, together with a slow stretch and a deep breath, can help them disappear more quickly.

questions.stem: Why might scientists still disagree about why people yawn?

Because there are two reasonable ideas and no single proven answer yet

Because only children are able to yawn at all, according to some people

wrong.C: The article suggests yawning happens often, not once a year.

questions.stem: Why does the author describe yawning before describing hiccups?
options: To explain two different, puzzling body reflexes one at a time
To prove that yawning is more dangerous than hiccups
To show that yawning always causes hiccups afterward
To argue that only hiccups are truly worth any scientific study at all

wrong.B: The article does not rank one as more dangerous.
wrong.C: Yawning is not shown to cause hiccups.
wrong.D: Both reflexes are treated as worth explaining.

MID.prompt: Explain how yawning and hiccups are alike and different. Use the words contagious and spasm in your answer.
checklist: I explained something yawning and hiccups have in common.
I explained one way they are different.
I used the words contagious and spasm correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Yawning and hiccups are alike because they are both involuntary reflexes that the body does without being asked. However, they are different in other ways: yawning is contagious and can spread just from seeing or hearing someone else yawn, while a hiccup happens when the diaphragm has a sudden spasm, making the vocal cords snap shut and produce the 'hic' sound.

questions.stem: According to the article, which nerve controls the diaphragm?

A nerve that controls breathing

A type of gas that is commonly found inside carbonated soft drinks

questions.stem: In the article, the word hypothesis refers to —

a type of muscle spasm in the body
a proven medical fact that no scientist disputes
a specific nerve pathway that directly connects the brain to the diaphragm muscle

questions.stem: Why do scientists describe the brain-cooling idea and the alertness idea as hypotheses rather than facts?
options: Because both of these competing ideas were already proven completely false by researchers long ago
Because yawning has never been studied by any scientist

Because neither idea has been fully confirmed as the single correct explanation
questions.why: The article presents both explanations as possibilities, not confirmed facts, which is why they remain hypotheses.

wrong.A: The article does not say either idea was proven false.
wrong.B: The article describes ongoing scientific interest in yawning.
wrong.C: The two ideas describe different possible functions of a yawn.

questions.stem: How are yawning and hiccups similar, based on the article?
options: Both are involuntary reflexes that a person cannot simply choose to start or stop
Both are caused only by drinking carbonated beverages

Both of these reflexes are controlled entirely and completely by the glottis alone

questions.stem: A researcher notices that watching a video of someone yawning makes test subjects yawn as well. Which idea from the article does this observation best support?

questions.stem: Why does the author present two separate hypotheses about yawning instead of just one?
options: To prove that one of the ideas is completely wrong

HIGH.prompt: Explain the chain of events inside the body during a hiccup, from the phrenic nerve to the final 'hic' sound. Then explain why scientists still consider yawning only partly explained.
checklist: I explained the chain of events during a hiccup, including the phrenic nerve and the glottis.
I explained why yawning is still only partly explained by scientists.
I used at least three key words from the article correctly.
HIGH.modelAnswer: During a hiccup, the phrenic nerve sends a confused signal to the diaphragm, causing it to spasm suddenly as an involuntary reflex. This sudden spasm makes the glottis, the small opening between the vocal cords, snap shut quickly, which produces the familiar 'hic' sound. Yawning remains only partly explained because scientists have proposed two competing hypotheses, brain cooling and rising alertness, but neither has been confirmed as the single correct explanation.
